# Budd-Chiari syndrome

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the liver > Budd-Chiari syndrome*

[Original Article Link](/library/LL0wyg)

---

## Summary

Budd-Chiari syndrome (BCS) is a rare condition characterized by <u>hepatic vein</u> obstruction that manifests with <u>hepatomegaly</u>, <u>ascites</u>, and abdominal discomfort. BCS is most commonly caused by <u>thrombotic</u> occlusion secondary to a chronic <u>myeloproliferative neoplasm</u> (e.g., <u>polycythemia vera</u>). Blood flow obstruction causes <u>liver</u> congestion and subsequent <u>liver</u> cell damage. If left untreated, patients may develop <u>liver</u> failure. Diagnosis is confirmed based on <u>cross-sectional imaging</u> (e.g., <u>Doppler ultrasound</u>). Management should be specialist-guided and include a strategy for restoring hepatic venous outflow with anticoagulation with or without invasive therapy (e.g., <u>balloon angioplasty</u>, or <u>TIPS</u>). <u>Liver transplant</u> should be considered if other treatments are unsuccessful. Additionally, underlying causes and complications (e.g., <u>portal hypertension</u>, <u>variceal bleeding</u>) should be managed.

---

## Etiology

<u>BCS</u> is characterized by <u>hepatic vein</u> obstruction, which is <u>idiopathic</u> in approx. 20% of cases or occurs secondary to: [[1]](/library/u4dpOJ0)




* Conditions associated with <u>hypercoagulability</u> (most common) [[1]](/library/u4dpOJ0)[[2]](/library/_0X5i9)

* <u>Myeloproliferative neoplasms</u>, e.g.:

* <u>Polycythemia vera</u> (most common cause)

* <u>Essential thrombocythemia</u>

* <u>Antiphospholipid syndrome</u>

* <u>Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria</u>

* Paraneoplastic <u>thrombocytosis</u>

* <u>Pregnancy</u> and <u>postpartum period</u>

* Inherited clotting disorders (e.g., <u>factor V Leiden</u> <u>thrombophilia</u>)

* Chronic inflammatory diseases (e.g., <u>Behcet disease</u>)

* Adverse effect of medication (e.g., <u>hormonal contraception</u>)

* Invasion or compression of the <u>hepatic veins</u>

* <u>Hepatocellular carcinoma</u> (<u>HCC</u>)

* <u>Renal cell carcinoma</u>

* Chronic infections (e.g., <u>amebiasis</u>, <u>aspergillosis</u>, <u>syphilis</u>, <u>tuberculosis</u>)

* Hepatic lesions

---

## Pathophysiology

* Obstruction (e.g., due to <u>thrombosis</u> or compression) of <u>hepatic veins</u> → ↓ blood outflow → hepatic venous congestion → increased sinusoidal pressure, cellular <u>hypoxia</u>, centrilobular necrosis   → <u>congestive hepatopathy</u>

* May develop into “<u>nutmeg liver</u>”:  Because of <u>ischemia</u> and fatty degeneration, the tissue appears speckled with dark spots.

* Clinical symptoms depend on the extent of hepatic injury and <u>portal hypertension</u>.

---

## Clinical features

* Abdominal <u>pain</u>

* Tender <u>hepatomegaly</u>

* <u>Ascites</u> and abdominal distention

* <u>Jaundice</u>

* Signs of increased <u>perfusion</u> of <u>portocaval anastomoses</u> (e.g., <u>esophageal varices</u>, or <u>caput medusae</u>)

* In severe cases: ankle <u>edema</u>, <u>splenomegaly</u>, and renal impairment





![Caput medusae and ascites](media/sc8z429r17o2b0do1iohek24.jpg)

Caput medusae and ascites




> [!NOTE]
> In contrast to <u>congestive heart failure</u>, which can also cause hepatic congestion, Budd-Chiari syndrome does not lead to <u>jugular venous distension</u>.




References: [[4]](/library/GfYBno)

---

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)[[6]](/library/mBXVY00)




Consider BCS in all patients with unexplained <u>acute liver failure</u> or <u>chronic liver disease</u>.  [[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)




* Diagnosis is confirmed by hepatic venous flow obstruction on imaging studies.

* Hepatic <u>venography</u> and <u>liver biopsy</u> are not usually required for diagnostic confirmation.

* Further studies are needed to evaluate for underlying causes, e.g., <u>thrombophilia</u>.

* Consult hepatology and/or <u>hematology</u> as needed in cases of diagnostic uncertainty.





> [!TIP]
> BCS presentations are highly variable (i.e., acute, chronic, or acute-on-chronic), and clinical and laboratory findings are nonspecific. [[1]](/library/u4dpOJ0)[[6]](/library/mBXVY00)




### Imaging studies [[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)[[6]](/library/mBXVY00)




* <u>Doppler ultrasound</u> [[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)

* Obtain for all patients with suspected BCS (preferred initial test).

* Findings of hepatic venous obstruction include:  [[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)[[6]](/library/mBXVY00)

* Presence of a <u>thrombus</u>

* Nonvisible <u>hepatic vein</u>  [[6]](/library/mBXVY00)

* Collateral <u>veins</u>

* Enlarged caudate <u>vein</u> diameter (> 3 mm)

* <u>Caudate lobe</u> <u>hypertrophy</u>

* Additional findings may include <u>adenomas</u>, nodular <u>hyperplasia</u>, or signs of <u>HCC</u>.

* CT with contrast or <u>MRI</u> scan is indicated for: [[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)

* Further characterization of lesions, including:

* <u>Thrombus</u> on <u>Doppler ultrasound</u>  [[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)

* Indeterminate hepatic <u>nodules</u>  [[6]](/library/mBXVY00)

* Inconclusive <u>Doppler ultrasound</u> in patients with high clinical suspicion [[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)

* Therapeutic assessment to determine response to anticoagulation therapy





![Hepatic venous obstruction in Budd-Chiari syndrome](media/onv90vlw8nh89raiawatbny6.jpg)

Hepatic venous obstruction in Budd-Chiari syndrome




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)[[6]](/library/mBXVY00)




* <u>Liver</u> disease workup (findings are nonspecific)

* Blood tests [[6]](/library/mBXVY00)

* <u>Elevated transaminases</u>  [[1]](/library/u4dpOJ0)

* ↑ <u>Bilirubin</u>

* ↓ <u>Albumin</u> and ↓ total protein

* ↑ <u>Prothrombin</u> time (↑ <u>INR</u>) in advanced cases

* <u>Hyponatremia</u>

* <u>Ascites</u> fluid analysis [[7]](/library/BTXzGx)[[8]](/library/Lccw1Y0)

* <u>High SAAG ascites</u>

* ↑ Protein levels > 2.5 g/dL in early BCS (may be low in later stages of the disease) [[8]](/library/Lccw1Y0)

* <u>Thrombophilia workup</u>: for all patients with confirmed BCS [[6]](/library/mBXVY00)

* Consult <u>hematology</u>.

* Obtain workup for <u>hereditary thrombophilia</u> and <u>acquired thrombophilia</u> (see “Etiology” for most common causes).

* Additional factors should be investigated even if a single causal factor is identified.

---

## Treatment

### General principles [[1]](/library/u4dpOJ0)[[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)




* Restoration of the hepatic venous outflow (e.g., using anticoagulation or invasive methods)

* Management of the underlying cause (e.g., <u>thrombophilia</u>)

* Management of complications (e.g., <u>portal hypertension</u>; , <u>variceal bleeding</u>, <u>ascites</u>, <u>acute liver failure</u>)

* Consult hepatology, <u>hematology</u>, and other specialties as needed.





> [!TIP]
> A stepwise treatment approach from least invasive (e.g., anticoagulation) to most invasive (e.g., <u>liver transplant</u>) is usually recommended. [[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)




### Noninvasive therapy [[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)[[6]](/library/mBXVY00)




* Long-term <u>anticoagulant</u> therapy: initial treatment of choice [[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)[[6]](/library/mBXVY00)

* Recommended for all patients regardless of the underlying cause [[6]](/library/mBXVY00)

* <u>Gastroesophageal varices</u> are not a contraindication for <u>anticoagulant</u> use. [[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)

* Recommended regimen: initial therapy with <u>LMWH</u>, followed by <u>VKA</u>  [[6]](/library/mBXVY00)

* <u>Treatment of portal hypertension</u> (as indicated for patients with <u>cirrhosis</u>): e.g., <u>diuretics</u>, <u>nonselective beta blockers</u> for prophylaxis of <u>variceal bleeding</u>  [[1]](/library/u4dpOJ0)[[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)





### Invasive therapy [[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)[[6]](/library/mBXVY00)




Invasive therapy is usually indicated if noninvasive approaches have been unsuccessful. [[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)[[6]](/library/mBXVY00)




* Recanalization of obstructed vessels, including:

* <u>Balloon angioplasty</u> ± <u>stenting</u> of the <u>hepatic vein</u>: most effective for short-segment <u>hepatic vein</u> obstruction

* Localized <u>thrombolysis</u> (low success rate) : may be useful for acute <u>stent</u> or <u>TIPS</u> <u>thrombosis</u>  [[5]](/library/84dOOJ0)

* Shunts:  to decompress the <u>hepatic sinusoids</u>: i.e., <u>TIPS</u>, <u>direct intrahepatic portosystemic shunts</u> , or surgical <u>portosystemic shunts</u> [[6]](/library/mBXVY00)

* <u>Liver transplant</u>

* For patients with <u>liver</u> failure or if less invasive approaches are unsuccessful

* Curative for selected prothrombotic diseases, e.g., <u>protein C deficiency</u> or <u>protein S deficiency</u>  [[1]](/library/u4dpOJ0)
